lessons.title: Who Can Claim the HRA Exemption: Conditions, Tax Regime and Salary Structure

body.text: Receiving HRA does not mean you can claim the HRA exemption. You have to pass four tests, every one of them, for every month you claim. Fail one and the whole allowance is taxed like the rest of your salary.

children.text: Every January, HR teams across Bengaluru and Gurugram send out the same reminder: submit your rent receipts. Thousands of employees upload receipts without checking whether they qualify at all. Some are on the new regime, some live in their own flat, some pay rent to a spouse. Their claims are either rejected by the employer or, worse, accepted and later questioned by the tax department. This lesson gives you the test to run before you claim.
The Four Tests

The exemption under Schedule III (Table: S. No. 11) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 10(13A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961) comes with conditions that fall into four simple questions. Answer yes to all four and you are eligible. The amount you can claim is a separate calculation, covered in Chapter 2.
Test 1: Are you a salaried employee who receives HRA?

The exemption applies only to House Rent Allowance paid by an employer as part of salary. A freelancer, consultant, business owner or pensioner receives no HRA, so there is nothing to exempt. Equally, an employee whose CTC has no HRA line, perhaps because everything sits in basic and special allowance, cannot claim it either.

body.text: Paying rent but not receiving HRA? A separate rent deduction exists for you, known as Section 80GG under the 1961 Act. It is capped at ₹60,000 a year and also works only under the old regime. Lesson 12 covers it.

children.text: Test 2: Are you on the old tax regime for this tax year?

markDefs.definition: The default tax regime under Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act). It has lower slab rates and a larger standard deduction but does not allow most exemptions and deductions, including HRA.
The regime with higher slab rates that still allows exemptions and deductions such as HRA, Section 80C, Section 80D and home loan interest. Salaried individuals must actively choose it.

body.text: The old regime must be chosen in a return filed by the due date, generally 31 July for salaried individuals whose accounts are not audited. Miss the deadline and you lose the option for that year, so your HRA exemption goes with it.

children.text: Test 3: Do you actually pay rent for the home you live in?

The rent must be real, paid by you and for the house you occupy. Living rent-free with parents, in a relative's flat or in company-provided accommodation fails this test. So does paying rent for a flat you do not live in, such as one your parents occupy in your hometown while you live in a hostel near your office.
Test 4: Is the home you live in owned by someone else?

You cannot pay rent to yourself. If you live in a flat you own, even partly, there is no exemption for that home. Owning a house somewhere else is a different story. An employee who owns a flat in Nagpur but rents in Hyderabad for work passes this test, because the home they live in belongs to someone else.

body.label: All four tests, month by month
body.context: The exemption applies only for the months in which you receive HRA and pay rent for a home you occupy and do not own. A single "no" means that month's HRA is fully taxable.

body.text: Owning a house in the same city where you rent is not banned, but it is a red flag. If you own a 2BHK in Andheri and rent another flat in Powai, be ready to explain why, for example the owned flat is let out, too far from work or too small for your family. Keep the evidence.

body.title: Quick Check: The Hometown Flat
body.question: Rahul works for a bank in Hyderabad and rents a flat in Madhapur for ₹28,000 a month. He owns a flat in Nagpur, where his parents live. He receives HRA and has chosen the old regime. Can he claim the HRA exemption?
options: No, because he already owns a house
Yes, because the flat he lives in is rented and he does not own it
Only if he sells the Nagpur flat
body.explanation: The fourth test asks whether you own the home you live in, not whether you own any house at all. Rahul lives in a rented flat in Hyderabad and pays the rent himself, so he passes all four tests. Owning a flat in another city does not stop the exemption. Lesson 10 shows how he may also claim tax benefits on a home loan for the Nagpur flat.

body.title: Quick Check: The Company Flat
body.question: Farhan moved to Kolkata on a transfer. His employer leases a flat for him and pays the landlord directly. His payslip has no HRA line. What is the correct tax treatment?
options: He can claim HRA exemption on the rent his employer pays
He can claim Section 80GG on the rent his employer pays
HRA exemption does not apply, because he receives no HRA and pays no rent himself
He can claim HRA exemption if he opts for the old regime
body.explanation: Farhan fails Test 1 (no HRA) and Test 3 (he pays no rent). Accommodation provided by an employer is taxed separately as a perquisite, valued under the rules for rent-free or concessional housing. It is a different mechanism from HRA, and he cannot use the rent deduction either, because he is not the one paying rent.

children.text: Month by Month: When the Tests Change During the Year

Eligibility is not a once-a-year yes or no. The exemption is worked out only for the period in which you both receive HRA and pay rent. New joiners, people who move out of their parents' home and people who buy a flat mid-year will pass the tests for some months and fail them for others.

body.title: Scenario: The Mid-Year Joiner
body.scenario: Priyanka joins a fintech firm in Bengaluru on 1 October 2026 and chooses the old regime. For October and November she stays with her aunt in Jayanagar and pays nothing. From 1 December she rents a flat in Indiranagar for ₹30,000 a month. Her HRA from the new employer is ₹22,000 a month from October onwards. Before joining, she was a full-time MBA student with no salary.
body.prompt: For which months of tax year 2026-27 can Priyanka claim the HRA exemption, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Only December 2026 to March 2027, four months in total. From April to September 2026 she had no salary and no HRA, so Test 1 fails. In October and November she received HRA but paid no rent, so Test 3 fails, and her ₹44,000 of HRA for those two months is fully taxable. From December she passes all four tests, so the exemption is calculated on the four months of HRA (₹88,000) and rent (₹1,20,000), using salary for those same four months. Chapter 2 shows the calculation, and Lesson 8 covers these part-year cases in detail. She must also make sure her employer knows the rent started in December, so TDS is not calculated as if she paid rent from October.

children.text: Eligible Is Not the Same as Worth It

Passing the four tests tells you the exemption is available. It does not tell you the old regime will save you money. Under the new regime, a salaried person with no other income pays zero tax on salary up to ₹12.75 lakh, thanks to the ₹75,000 standard deduction and the rebate. For many employees below that level, claiming HRA means choosing a regime that costs more.

body.label: Zero-tax salary under the new regime
body.context: Tax year 2026-27, salary as the only income: ₹75,000 standard deduction brings taxable income to ₹12 lakh, and the rebate wipes out the tax on it.

body.title: Neha in Kolkata: gross salary ₹11,00,000, eligible HRA exemption ₹1,50,000, Section 80C ₹1,50,000

children.text: Neha is fully eligible for HRA, and it still makes no sense for her to claim it. Even with her HRA and 80C claims, the old regime costs her ₹65,000 more than the new regime. The HRA exemption becomes valuable at higher salaries, higher rents and alongside other deductions. Our course on choosing between the old and new regimes shows how to find your breakeven.

body.title: Try It: Neha Without HRA
body.prompt: Suppose Neha stayed in the old regime but could not claim HRA, for example because she moved in with her parents. Her other figures stay the same: gross salary ₹11,00,000, standard deduction ₹50,000 and Section 80C ₹1,50,000. What would her tax be under the old regime, including 4% cess? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Taxable income rises to ₹9,00,000. Tax is 5% of ₹2,50,000 (₹12,500) plus 20% of ₹4,00,000 (₹80,000), which is ₹92,500. Adding 4% cess gives ₹96,200. So her HRA exemption is worth ₹31,200 in the old regime (₹96,200 minus ₹65,000), but the new regime still beats both options at zero tax.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Silent Default
body.textWithBlank: If you do not tell your employer which regime you want, TDS on your salary is calculated under the ___ tax regime, and your rent is ignored.
body.explanation: The new regime under Section 202 is the default. Without your declaration, your employer must assume you have not opted out, so no HRA exemption is given in your monthly TDS. You can still choose the old regime in your return if you file by the due date, but you may end up paying the extra tax upfront through TDS and waiting for a refund.

children.text: Run the Test on Yourself

body.title: Your HRA Eligibility Check
steps: Open your payslip and confirm there is a House Rent Allowance line with a non-zero amount
Log in to your HR portal and check which tax regime you declared for tax year 2026-27
Confirm you pay rent yourself, by bank transfer or UPI, for the home you actually live in
Confirm you do not own, fully or partly, the home you live in
If you own another house in the same city, write down why you rent instead and keep supporting documents
Mark the months this year in which all four tests were met. Those are the only months you can claim

cards.definition: To claim HRA exemption you must receive HRA, be on the old regime, actually pay rent for the home you live in, and not own that home.
The regime that allows exemptions and deductions such as HRA and Section 80C. Salaried employees must opt for it, both with the employer for TDS and in their return.
The provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025 that makes the new tax regime the default. It corresponds to Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act.
The provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025 under which employers deduct TDS from salary. It corresponds to Section 192 of the 1961 Act.
A non-cash benefit from an employer, such as a company-leased flat, which is taxed under its own valuation rules instead of as HRA.
Known as Section 80GG under the 1961 Act. It lets people who pay rent but receive no HRA claim up to ₹60,000 a year under the old regime.

points: HRA exemption needs four yeses: you receive HRA, you are on the old regime, you pay rent for the home you live in, and you do not own that home
Freelancers, business owners and employees without an HRA component cannot claim HRA exemption, though they may qualify for the separate rent deduction
The new regime is the default. Declare the old regime to your employer for correct TDS, and choose it in a return filed by the due date to lock in the exemption
Owning a house in another city does not block HRA. Owning one in the same city is allowed but invites questions
Eligibility is tested month by month, so new joiners and people who start renting mid-year claim only for the qualifying months
Being eligible does not make HRA worth claiming. Below ₹12.75 lakh of salary, the new regime usually costs nothing at all
